know.title: Team is people, Group is data
know.body: A Team is who they work with. A Group can decide which sites, MPANs, reports, and documents they inherit. Do not treat them as the same thing.

done.note: Operational is trading. Non-operational is people may be there, not trading. Closed is shut. Hours ticks cut the graph and Breakdown.

done.note: This day last month to today. The number of days follows the calendar, so a longer month keeps the 29th, 30th, or 31st.

notes.text: Version one has to do enough of what DataVision does or the move will fail.

Clive and Emily Haddon did a dozen plus customer interviews. Those notes sit with Clive.

Version one of the tree is simple. Alexi marked electricity and gas. Import and export would be tags later. Water has never been tested.
Site address is read only. Site name can be edited. Times of use means on peak and off peak, not terms of use.
They log into the new customer portal, not the admin beast. About a third of the left icons show, depending on access. DataVision makes them find a client first. This portal lets them click around.
Dashboard widgets can be dragged, not resized. James's later picture was a drag and drop graphical home, then a details page whose core cards stay on, then reports without the tree.
A premium customer can rebrand the portal. James mocked an Octopus skin in Figma. Enterprise customers on the old stack had their own colours and features switched on and off.
Shaun is walking DataVision with Max so the old screens sit next to James's new portal, not as a rumour.
Premium branding is still open. Either a styles page where they pick colours, or one stylesheet and no picker. James showed the picker. Clive decides.
If site attributes change over time, area, capacity, and emissions reports have to follow the date. James thinks that is extra version one work, not a given.
They pick sites and meters, compare them to each other or to a fixed number, then export a file. They do not stare at the whole portfolio.

A site is a physical address. Nested sites exist, like flats in a tower. A fiscal meter counts power into the building. Submeters count rooms. Adding both into the site total double counts unless a flag says to.
Someone higher in the chain can look down. EDF can see Network Rail. Network Rail cannot look up or sideways at EDF's other customers.
Astral already has scheduled reports and alerts. DataVision also lets them pull an ad hoc interval report. Estimated versus actual is a real versus guessed reading.
Alexi is checking that Dev has users who can actually open the customer portal, with the right groups, so smoke tests mean something.
Clive would rather be late by a week or two than ship a bodge and start again in January.
British Gas and Scottish Water asked to beta. Clive will invite you to the customer migration stream.
UAT may have no consumption data until the pipeline actually runs.
Interval reports are the job. Max ignores a mostly blank dashboard and goes straight to the tree.
IMSERV masters site names. Import is the default. Export is written on the site name.
DataVision splits one physical site into two rows with two MPANs. A meter can count both ways.

Astral is not DataVision rebuilt in React. It is becoming the place a customer goes for energy data and outputs. Visualisation, portfolio, documents, permissions, and later contract-driven access sit together.
Three access questions. What has this company bought. What can this person do. Which sites, MPANs, reports, and documents can they see. Do not design one permissions blob.

insights.title: Client setup is highly manual
insights.problem: Setting up a new client means V moves information between several systems and keeps progress in her head.
insights.where: CRM and email into DataVision, then her tracking spreadsheet, then back to Data Provision.
insights.why: Teams did not all use the same system, so work still arrives in emails and she handles it by hand. She said the current walk works, and that much of it is still manual.
insights.note: The process depends on one person remembering where everything is and what stage each client has reached.

insights.title: There is no built-in way to track client setup progress
insights.problem: DataVision does not show what is set up, what is waiting for data, and what still needs action, so V made her own spreadsheet.
insights.why: She records client IDs, company details, dates, and users herself so she can search previous work and see what she has finished. She said this exists because there was no process or tracking in the product.
insights.note: This is a shadow system outside the product, and the walk depends on V's personal process.

insights.title: The same information has to be entered more than once
insights.problem: Contract dates often need updating at the client, then again against each user.
insights.why: On the renewal walk, V updated the contract end date and then the user's active-to date. She said this duplication happens a lot.
insights.note: Extra effort, and a risk that one date moves while the other stays.

insights.title: Access-date rules are difficult to understand
insights.problem: Access rules change depending on whether the person works for the customer or is an external third party.
insights.why: A customer employee normally inherits access from the company contract. A third-party user's access depends on a separate LOA expiry. V said understanding those dates took time because the model is complicated.
insights.note: This affects data access. Get it wrong and you get security and GDPR trouble.

insights.title: Contract information is fragmented across systems
insights.problem: The document that proves why a date or access change exists may live somewhere different from where the change is made.
insights.where: CRM, Fire Safe, V's local filing, and DataVision.
insights.why: V said contracts should be stored centrally, but historical contracts have sometimes been hard to find. She needs written evidence before she changes access dates, so she keeps her own copies as a fallback.
insights.note: The walk works largely because V fills the gaps.

insights.title: Third-party user management may be solving the wrong problem
insights.problem: IMSERV sometimes creates third-party users and manages their LOAs even when those people only need to receive customer data.
insights.why: V said the intended walk was often for the customer to schedule reports straight to third parties. That would avoid IMSERV creating accounts and managing LOAs for people it has no direct relationship with.
insights.note: Bigger than a UI issue. Part of the current walk may not need to exist.

insights.title: LOA management creates avoidable operational and data-access risk
insights.problem: Once IMSERV manages a third party's access, it also has to make sure that access stops when it should.
insights.why: V said scheduled reports controlled by the customer would remove much of the need for IMSERV to manage these relationships. The current walk creates risk if access or reporting continues after things change.
insights.note: This is governance and possibly GDPR. Treat it as a design constraint, not just an inconvenience.

insights.title: Duplicate companies can be created because matching is weak
insights.problem: The system does not reliably see that slightly different company names are the same organisation.
insights.example: Example Limited and Example LTD could be treated as different clients.
insights.why: V searches DataVision when she recognises a name, because something presented as new can be an existing client or a renewal.
insights.note: The safety net is V's experience and memory, not the system.

insights.title: The workflow depends heavily on specialist knowledge
insights.problem: V has years of knowledge about how DataVision, contracts, portfolios, users, and external systems fit together.
insights.why: The wider team described V as one of the remaining people who understands DataVision under the bonnet, and the person people go to when clients need setting up or when day to day problems arise.
insights.note: Part of the system logic lives in a person. That is a major migration risk.

insights.title: Customer onboarding is spread across too many systems
insights.problem: The onboarding team has to move between several systems to finish one customer setup.
insights.where: Supplier and customer onboarding across spreadsheets, Access databases, Panorama, Star, MOP Views, Fuse, Click, DataVision, and email.
insights.why: Katie repeatedly moved between tools to validate contracts, create services, create identifiers, check jobs, configure data access, and finally get information visible to the customer. Much of this has to be coordinated by hand.
insights.note: The walk is fragmented, hard to learn, and creates many chances for information to fall between systems.

insights.title: Job validation is extremely manual
insights.problem: Before raising installation or meter jobs, staff have to decide by hand whether the job is actually required.
insights.where: Supplier loader, then onboarding validation, then Fuse and job creation.
insights.why: Suppliers can send spreadsheets with tens to thousands of MPANs. Staff have to check whether IMSERV is appointed, whether a job already exists, whether a previous job failed, and whether the same contact details caused a previous failure. Katie gave the example of a withdrawn job being sent again with exactly the same contact information.
insights.note: At large volumes, checking individual MPANs by hand is unrealistic and raises avoidable work.

insights.title: The system does not make previous failures useful enough
insights.problem: Historic job information exists, but staff cannot easily use it to stop the same failed job being created again.
insights.where: Job onboarding and previous job history.
insights.why: Katie wanted to see that a previous job had been withdrawn because of incorrect contact details, compare that with the new details, and stop the same job being raised again. That still means inspecting historic records by hand.
insights.note: The information exists, but it is not turned into a useful decision. A future system could warn that a previous job was withdrawn for incorrect contact details, and that the new submission has the same contact information.

insights.title: Large supplier batches make the current workflow unscalable
insights.problem: The same manual validation is used whether the team receives 55 MPANs or thousands.
insights.why: Katie contrasted a small Octopus batch with a British Gas batch of thousands of MPANs. The team does not have the people to inspect every historic job one by one.
insights.note: This is not just an inconvenience. The current walk struggles as portfolio size grows.

insights.title: New customer setup requires duplicate manual configuration
insights.problem: The same customer has to be created and configured separately in more than one system.
insights.why: Katie described creating the customer and service in Panorama, then setting them up again in Star, including participant IDs, service configuration, and other records. She said these stages are entirely manual.
insights.note: This adds setup time and creates the chance that two systems no longer agree about the same customer.

insights.title: Staff must manually invent and manage technical identifiers
insights.problem: The onboarding team has to find unused identifiers and create records by hand.
insights.why: Katie described searching for an unused participant ID, creating it, linking it to a customer, and configuring the associated services.
insights.note: This is technical system administration pushed onto an operational user. The platform should generate or manage these identifiers behind the scenes.

insights.title: DataVision can show estimated data even when actual data exists
insights.problem: The customer can keep seeing estimated data even when better actual readings already exist elsewhere.
insights.why: Katie said DataVision effectively checks whether it already has data, rather than whether newer, more accurate data exists. Actual readings in Star therefore do not automatically replace estimated readings in DataVision.
insights.note: This directly affects the accuracy of what customers see. The platform can knowingly display worse data than the business already has.

insights.title: Correcting stale data requires a specialist manual reset
insights.problem: Staff cannot simply refresh incorrect DataVision data.
insights.why: If estimated data needs replacing, V may need to raise a ticket with Schneider, have existing DataVision data wiped, run an export from Star by hand, and repopulate DataVision.
insights.note: A basic data refresh depends on several people and systems. The new system should treat actual as better than estimated, and replace lower-quality data when authoritative data arrives.

insights.title: MPANs sometimes fail to appear without explanation
insights.problem: MPANs that should be visible to a customer sometimes do not appear.
insights.why: Katie described setups that look correct, but the MPAN does not appear in DataVision. The workaround can be deleting part of the configuration, recreating it, and rerunning an extract in the hope that it reloads.
insights.note: The user has no clear diagnosis or recovery path. This is a candidate for a future sync status, not a delete-and-recreate ritual.

insights.title: Contract termination and reactivation can leave unclear data-access states
insights.problem: An MPAN can be terminated and later reopened, but historic end dates may interfere with current access or data visibility.
insights.why: Katie showed an MPAN that had been terminated and later reopened. On paper the new access dates looked valid, but DataVision still had an issue and nobody could immediately explain why.
insights.note: The system does not clearly model terminated, re-contracted, currently active, and historic access periods. That matters when deciding which historic data a customer should see.

insights.title: Operational staff cannot easily diagnose why something is broken
insights.problem: When data or access fails, users can see the symptom but not the cause.
insights.where: Across Star, DataVision, and contract configuration.
insights.why: Several times Katie could see that something was wrong but could not tell why from the available information. Troubleshooting depended on V, Schneider, or further manual investigation.
insights.note: The future platform should expose states such as waiting for source data, MPAN not appointed, contract expired, awaiting sync, actual data available, data import failed, and user access expired, rather than only showing that something is missing.

insights.title: Customer onboarding depends on hand-offs between individual people
insights.problem: One person's setup work frequently becomes another person's manual input.
insights.where: Onboarding team to V to DataVision.
insights.why: Katie creates information and identifiers that are then passed to V, who does another set of manual setup steps to make the customer visible in DataVision.
insights.note: This introduces delays and makes the process depend on individual availability. It connects to V's walk, so both sides of the same hand-off are now named.

insights.title: Entitlement, role, and scope get mixed into one permissions idea
insights.problem: A person's experience is controlled by what the company bought, what that person can do, and which data they can see. Designing those as one blob makes user management hard to reason about.
insights.why: The handoff named three separate layers. Product entitlement is documents only or full Astral. Role is Admin, Manager, Contributor, or Viewer. Group membership can decide which sites, MPANs, reports, and documents they see.
insights.note: Ask Anthony before you design a single permissions page. The exact role matrix is still open.

insights.title: Huge portfolios cannot be treated as a long list
insights.problem: A customer can sit on thousands of MPANs. Loading them all, drawing thousands of series, or showing thousands of ticks will fail.
insights.why: The handoff named about 8,000 MPANs on a customer and about 45,000 on internal access. Max wants people to start with what is happening, then narrow to a place.
insights.note: Progressive disclosure already sits on the walk. All, then group, then site, then MPAN. Do not dump the whole estate.

insights.title: Teams and Groups get treated as the same thing
insights.problem: People groups and data groups were muddled in talks. Treating them as identical will produce a permissions spaghetti.
insights.where: Users, Portfolio tree, reports, and documents.
insights.why: The handoff said teams are mostly for workflow. Group membership can decide which MPANs, reports, and documents someone sees. An MPAN can sit in more than one group.
insights.note: Team is who I work with. Group is what I can access. They might later link. The final model is still open. Ask Max and Anthony. Permission user groups stay in admin.

insights.title: The shell cannot assume every login gets Portfolio
insights.problem: A documents-only customer may log in and see My Documents, notifications, and profile, with no energy walk.
insights.where: Navigation and first screen after sign in.
insights.why: Version one has two bought experiences. Documents only and full Astral. The entitlement is determined from sold services, not a customer pick.
insights.note: Hide Portfolio from a documents-only login. Self-serve upgrades wait. Do not design a huge entitlement UI that Super admin ticks by hand if the contract will do that work.

insights.title: Estimated readings and Alerts get the same pattern
insights.problem: A guessed reading and an abnormal reading are different states. Using the same mark mixes confidence with attention.
insights.why: The handoff named Estimated as we do not have an actual reading. Alert is unusually high, unusually low, or outside expected range. Version one alerts stay simple, such as high and low from the system.
insights.note: Estimated is confidence. Alert is attention. Odd use, Missing data, and Not sending stay on Alerts. Do not invent a statistical threshold builder for version one.

insights.title: Reports, documents, and exports get the same word
insights.problem: People and developers start talking about different files as if they were one thing.
insights.why: The handoff named four kinds. Scheduled report is clockwork from Astral. My Documents is a file IMSERV placed for the customer. Export is CSV or PDF from the current view. Data provision is the service behind those outputs.
insights.note: Keep scheduled reports off the documents pile. Keep My Documents off Downloads. Do not invent Excel.

groups.name: The band
groups.who: A small UK band using the product as themselves. Eyes of Home is the live example.
groups.need: Talk to fans in their own voice, get people to a gig, and see if a post actually worked.
groups.heard: As a band I want to get more people to buy tickets to a live show.
groups.open: Is the person writing captions the same person who puts the gig up?

notes.text: Asked for first person, the band speaking to their fans, not a marketing voice.
Built first as a one-band tool, not a multi-artist product.

journey.now: They are in the product as themselves. Eyes of Home is the live example.
They wanted first person, the band talking to fans, not a marketing voice.
They still cannot tell if a post actually worked.
Get people to a gig in their own voice.

groups.name: Someone buying a ticket
groups.who: A person going through checkout for a small gig, tested on an Eyes of Home show.
groups.need: A checkout that does not fight them, a price they trust, and a ticket they can scan on the door.
groups.heard: I think the QR code should be the first thing that comes up for ease of use.
groups.open: Did the confirmation email ever arrive, and what should My Gigs show first?

notes.text: Personal details felt cramped beside the order summary.
Raising the ticket count to 50 left the total stuck high after going back to one.
Apple Pay worked. The order page showed the ticket, but no email had come through yet.

journey.now: Checkout for a small gig, tested on an Eyes of Home show.
Personal details felt cramped beside the order summary. The total stuck high after changing the count.
The QR code should be the first thing that comes up.
A ticket they can scan on the door. Apple Pay worked. The email had not arrived yet.

groups.name: Someone checking if they can get in
groups.who: A person who needs a straight answer about the room before they buy.
groups.need: A plain sentence about access, not a yes or no flag.
groups.heard: It says accessibility, no. I think the message should be a bit better than that.
groups.open: We have one example about wheelchairs. What else does the room need to say?

notes.text: Wanted copy like there are no facilities for wheelchairs at the venue, not a bare no.

journey.now: They check the room before they buy.
